title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Sep 29, 2026
intro: Agent security and observability lead this week: keep secrets, traces, and tool-call chains out of the agent's reach.

cards.title: Inject secrets at the egress proxy, not into the sandbox
cards.problem: A secret placed in the agent sandbox can be read, logged, or exfiltrated by a prompt-injected agent.
cards.apply: Store each credential once in a secrets service, give the agent only an ID reference, and have an egress proxy add the real value to outbound requests.
cards.result: Google claims the agent can call authenticated APIs without ever holding the raw secret, which shrinks what a compromised run can leak.

evidence.note: Google states the Credentials API keeps secrets out of the agent sandbox.

cards.title: Drop sticky sessions from your remote MCP servers
cards.problem: Session-bound MCP servers force sticky routing and session storage, which blocks simple horizontal scaling.
cards.apply: Move remote MCP servers to the stateless spec revision: carry needed context in each request and remove session affinity and session-store config from your load balancer.
cards.result: AWS claims any instance can serve any request, so scaling and failover need no session-routing layer.

evidence.note: AWS describes the spec as removing protocol-level sessions and sticky-session requirements.

cards.title: Write agent traces where the agent cannot edit them
cards.problem: If the agent can modify its own trace, your audits and evals may be scoring a rewritten history.
cards.apply: Ship traces to an append-only store outside the agent sandbox, and give the agent no write or delete path to it.
cards.result: Trace-based debugging and evals rest on records the agent could not have altered.

evidence.note: Inferred from the source's claim that agents can tamper with their own traces.

cards.title: Flag injection by tool-call chain, not by email text alone
cards.problem: Injected instructions in retrieved email look like ordinary text, so content-only filters miss them.
cards.apply: Log which untrusted content preceded each tool call and flag sequences where retrieved content triggers a high-impact action such as sending or forwarding mail.
cards.result: Injection attempts get caught at the action that would cause harm, even when the text itself looks benign.

evidence.note: Inferred from the paper's attack-chain modeling approach for email agents.

cards.title: Review long agent runs as conversation-style trajectories
cards.problem: Raw span-level traces make it slow to find where a long-running agent went wrong.
cards.apply: Render each session as an ordered conversation of model turns and tool calls, and review failures from that view before digging into spans.
cards.result: LangChain claims a read-through of the trajectory replaces a span-tree hunt when root-causing a bad long-running session.

evidence.note: LangChain claims trajectories speed up debugging for long-running agents.

cards.title: Re-price your coding agent for long, high-context sessions
cards.problem: Long coding sessions re-send large contexts, so per-token price comparisons hide the real session cost.
cards.apply: Replay a representative long session against the new Opus and your current model, and compare total cost per completed task, not per-token price.
cards.result: You pick the model on cost per finished task for your actual session length.

evidence.note: Inferred from Anthropic pricing the model for longer, higher-context coding sessions.
